newsitem.title: USA: Perot says in presidential race to 'bitter end'.
newsitem.headline: Perot says in presidential race to 'bitter end'.

text.p: Reform Party candidate Ross Perot on Thursday ridiculed Republican Bob Dole's plea that he quit the presidential race and back Dole as "weird and totally inconsequential" and said he was in the race to stay.
"Am I in this for the long haul? Yes. Do I intend to campaign to the bitter end? Yes," Perot said in response to questions at a National Press Club appearance.

Asked about reports -- confirmed earlier by his own aides -- that Dole had sent an envoy to ask him to drop out and support the Republican challenger against Democratic President Bill Clinton, Perot said he would not divulge what had been said in a private conversation.
But the Texas billionaire bristled with annoyance at the focus given the Dole episode while he was trying to promote his own demands for campaign finance reform and a balanced federal budget.
He added: "Isn't it fascinating that ... if something weird and totally inconsequential pops up like this thing (involving Dole) yesterday, that is really big news, right?"

Asked if the appeal were a sign of desperation by Dole, who trails Clinton by double-digit figures in most polls with the election looming on Nov. 5, Perot said: "In no way do I want to do anything to harm another candidate's constructive campaign ... The thing I can assure you is that I am here, I am here to stay."
He spoke as U.S. political circles buzzed with astonishment at word that Dole had sent a top aide to make a pitch for help from Perot just 12 days before Election Day.

Only a month ago Dole's campaign led a successful effort to keep the sharp-tongued Texan out of televised Dole-Clinton campaign debates. That infuriated Perot, who is running a weak third in the polls and badly needed exposure in the debates.
The attention given Dole's request breathed new life into the Perot campaign, which had been fading from the political screen.

Perot's audience of about 160 press club luncheon guests was matched by almost as many reporters, photographers and cameramen drawn out by the Dole controversy. The event was televised nationally over CNN and the C-Span cable network.
While Perot spurned Dole's overture, he also took up some of his lines of attack on Clinton on ethical issues.

They included questionable campaign contributions to Democrats from associates of Indonesian, North Korean and other foreign interests, and over Clinton's refusal to promise he would not pardon former friends and business associates convicted of fraud charges in Arkansas.

"I never thought I would live to see a major drug dealer give 20,000 bucks in Florida ... and then be invited to the White House for a reception," said Perot, whose feisty, unvarnished style became familiar to Americans during his first and much stronger White House campaign four years ago.

He referred to a current dispute over a $20,000 campaign donation given in 1995 to the Democratic Party by one Jorge Cabrera, who was convicted on drug charges in the 1980s. He attended a White House reception last December.

Cabrera was arrested again in a drug bust last January involving some 6,000 pounds of cocaine. When stories about him surfaced recently, the Democratic National Committee gave his $20,000 donation to the U.S. Treasury.

"We are headed toward a second Watergate with all this stuff going on and a constitutional crisis in 1997, just remember where you heard it and put it in the bank," Perot told the Press Club audience.
